newsitem.title: USA: Golden Gate Bridge launches earthquake retrofit plan.
newsitem.headline: Golden Gate Bridge launches earthquake retrofit plan.

text.p: Officials on Tuesday launched a $175 million project to strengthen the world-famous Golden Gate Bridge to withstand major earthquakes.

Bridge officials said at a groundbreaking ceremony in San Francisco that the first phase of construction would cost $35 million and would be funded entirely with bridge toll revenues. They said they would seek another $140 million from the federal government to complete the work.
"The Golden Gate Bridge must have help to fund the remaining phases of retrofit construction," said John Fraser, president of the Golden Gate Bridge, Highway and Transportation District board.
The federal funds are needed because of the bridge's "vulnerability during earthquakes," Fraser said.

An earthquake measuring 7.0 or greater on the Richter scale on the San Andreas or Hayward faults, which lie within 10 miles (16 km) of the bridge, could have catastrophic results, bridge officials said.

Studies have shown that in a major earthquake the approaches to the Golden Gate Bridge could fail, an arch at the southern end of the bridge could jump off its bearings, the main span could slam against the bridge towers like a battering ram and the tower legs could buckle, they said.
The elegant suspension bridge which spans the mouth of San Francisco Bay carries 120,000 vehicles a day.

The first phase of construction -- expected to take 2-1/2 years to complete -- will retrofit the northern end of the bridge, considered to be the most vulnerable in a major earthquake, officials said.
Traffic crossing the bridge will not be impacted because construction will take place in areas under and adjacent to the bridge, they said.
If the federal government comes up with the $140 million by this fall, the entire four-phase project could be completed within three to five years, officials said.
If the federal government fails to authorize funding, the bridge could issue bonds to complete the project, they said.

The Golden Gate Bridge District commissioned seismic studies following the 7.1-magnitude Loma Prieta quake of October 1989, which killed 63 people and caused $6 billion of damage in the San Francisco Bay area.

The Golden Gate Bridge suffered no significant damage in that quake but many structures in the San Francisco area were badly damaged. Most of the victims died when the double-decker Cypress freeway in nearby Oakland collapsed.
